1:
The healing follows a rejection, and Chrysostom makes the connection deliberate: leaving the temple where his words were refused, Christ went where his absence might cool their fury and the miracle soften them. He notes the order of seeing — Christ saw the blind man, not the blind man Christ — and so intently that the disciples were struck. Henry draws the practical lesson: after such abuse he still missed no opportunity of doing good, and we make more haste than good speed when we outrun such opportunities. Bede and Augustine take the passing by as the descent from heaven and the man as the human race, blind from birth since the first man sinned.

The disciples' question is defended, explained and demolished by turns. Ellicott insists they bring it not for discussion but as a mystery of life in all its darkness, and warns that the form sets both alternatives on the same footing, so we may not assume they ruled either out. Theophylact finds it improper and hard to account for, the apostles never having been taught that a soul could sin before birth; Chrysostom traces it to the word spoken to the paralytic, sin no more, and thinks they asked less for information than from perplexity, as men exclaim over an ill-used child. Clarke surveys transmigration through Pythagoras, Josephus and Philo, and a Hindu schedule where blindness answers for having killed one's mother. Lightfoot dismantles it: on Josephus's account only good souls pass into other bodies, so unless one will say some good man's soul produced this blindness — which every man would cry shame of — the principle says nothing to the case.

The answer is guarded against proving too much. Augustine asks whether the man was born without original sin, and answers that both he and his parents had sinned, only that sin was not the reason for his blindness. Chrysostom will not concede he suffered unjustly, the blindness being a benefit that brought him to see with the inward eye, and adds that the word rendered that may express event rather than cause. Calvin names three errors: censuring others while winking at our own faults, reading any stroke as deadly hatred, and condemning all whom God visits, when Job was more wretched than any man not for sin but that his piety might be proved. Ellicott states it exactly — a chain connects humanity's sin with its woe, but the links are not traceable by the human eye — and Henry warns against accusing those whom God has justified.

On the working, Robertson settles a text: the true reading is we must work the works of him that sent me, joining the disciples to his own commission, and judges Bernard's defence of the singular vigorous but vain. Barnes makes the night death, with perhaps six months left to run. Calvin generalises: every man's life may be called his day, and as the short light drives labourers to industry, so we should be ashamed to languish in idleness. Wesley draws the sharp edge — no man can do anything toward his salvation once this life is ended, though Christ can work always — and Augustine says beyond that night is neither faith nor labour nor repentance.

The last clause is read as a limitation, then unlimited again. Ellicott says the true Light cannot be in the world without shining in its darkness. Calvin raises the difficulty that God's power shone more brightly through the preaching after Christ's death, and answers that having finished his own course he laboured no less powerfully by his ministers, his bodily presence having been the true day whose lustre reaches every age. Augustine puts it otherwise: the natural day is closed by the circuit of the sun, but the day of Christ's presence lasts to the end of the world, since he said, Lo, I am with you always.
6:
Why clay at all comes first, and nobody thinks it medicine. Chrysostom says he used spittle rather than water so nothing might afterwards be ascribed to the fountain, the power that formed the eyes proceeding from his own mouth. Clarke admits the difficulty and doubts any medical tendency, concluding that God works in his own way and hides pride from man by means often contrary to the end proposed; Wesley presses harder, that this treatment might almost have blinded a man who could see, God being no farther from the event when he works with means than without. Robertson cites Dods against the notion that virtue lay in the clay, since in other cures Christ used none.

Ellicott takes the opposite tack and lets the means be means. Pliny, Tacitus and Suetonius attest fasting saliva as a recognised remedy for the eyes, and the rabbis the same, so here the Divine is manifested through the human and an ordinary prescription meets what lay beyond human power — physicians had long treated blindness that came after birth, but blindness from birth was reckoned incurable. He records a second reading, as old as Irenaeus, that the clay recalls the creation of man from dust, the same power completing what was left unfinished.

The day supplies another motive. Lightfoot shows from the rabbis both that spittle was reckoned wholesome for weak eyes — in a tale where R. Meir feigns an ailment so a woman may spit seven times on him and discharge her husband's command — and that smearing the eyes with it was forbidden on the sabbath for any medicinal purpose. Barnes builds on that: Jesus deliberately did what they held unlawful, showing their keeping of the day superstitious and contrary to God's intention; Robertson adds that kneading the clay was a second offence. Barnes gives a further reason, that prophets commonly used expressive actions, so a man who could not see his healer might learn by touch whence the power came.

The sending to Siloam is read as a trial. Chrysostom asks why he was not told to wash at once, and answers that the Jews' obstinacy might be overcome by the sight of him walking there with clay on his eyes, that it proved Christ no enemy to the Law, and that no glory could accrue to the pool, many having washed there without benefit. Calvin makes it the trial of faith: the cure begins so absurdly that it seems to double the blindness, and any man would suspect mockery, yet on a bare word he goes — his faith the more commendable for resting on so small a knowledge, since he knew only that Christ was sent from God. Barnes finds the same test, setting him beside Naaman, the proud Syrian despising the direction while the humble blind man obeyed.

The gloss on the name divides them, and produces the chapter's most candid moment. Lightfoot uses it to identify the pool, the spring feeding an upper pool called Siloah, which does mean Sent, and a lower called Shelah, which does not. Chrysostom compares the rock in the wilderness that was Christ, the sudden rise of the water figuring his unexpected manifestation in the flesh, while Clarke reports the view that the fountain typified the Shiloh of Jacob's blessing. Barnes had printed exactly that in his own first edition and here withdraws it — the words come from different roots, Siloam from the verb to send and Shiloh meaning rest, and there is no evidence John had the prophecy in mind. Augustine reads the sequence sacramentally instead, the man anointed but not yet seeing as one made a catechumen, enlightened only when sent to the pool and washed.
8:
The neighbours cannot agree it is the same man, and that proves useful. Chrysostom says the suddenness made men incredulous, and turns the man's poverty into an argument: God heals even beggars with such care, choosing not the great but the meanest, and so stopping the mouths of his critics. Henry works the same thought as providence — it was well ordered that the man be a common beggar and therefore widely known, since the miracle was thereby better attested against those who would deny he had ever been blind. Calvin notes how impiety is ingenious in obscuring God's works, so the brighter the display the less credit it wins — yet the doubting served the miracle, drawing a fuller testimony from the man.

Ellicott corrects the text here: the better reading is not that they had seen he was blind but that he was a beggar, which Robertson and Clarke accept. Ellicott then makes a literary claim about the scene, that it has the form natural to a narrative from one who was there, and that John may have had it from the man's own lips — some struck by points of identity, others by the opened eyes lighting up the whole face. Augustine had said as much in a sentence, that his eyes being opened had altered his look.

The trade he left behind draws out the antiquarians. Lightfoot and Clarke give the formulas Jewish beggars used, which were not requests but offers: deserve something by me, that is, acquire merit by the alms you give; O ye tender-hearted, do yourselves good by me; and, for those come down in the world, look back and see what I have been, look upon me now and see what I am. Henry finds a lesson in the posture — when he could not go about he sat, and if we cannot work for God we must sit still quietly for him. Robertson notes he had his regular pitch, a familiar figure, but now his eyes are wide open.

His own answer settles it, and the manner is admired. Augustine hears gratitude in the two words, a denial having convicted him of ingratitude, and Chrysostom that he was neither ashamed of his former blindness nor afraid of the crowd. Chrysostom marks the exactness of his account: he does not say how the clay was made, since he could not see the spitting, but only what he knew — the anointing he could feel, the command he could hear. Clarke calls the relation simple and artless in the highest degree, noting the man says he made clay, not clay of spittle. Henry turns it into a duty: those who receive special instances of God's power should report them, his favours being lost upon us when they go no further.

The last question reaches past the answer. Henry distinguishes three motives in the question — curiosity, ill-will, a proclamation being out for his apprehension, and good-will in those who wished to find him. Chrysostom judges the worst of it, that they were already meditating his death, and explains the withdrawal: Christ never appeared with those he cured, so no suspicion might attach to the miracle and none could say the man published a false cure to oblige him. On the confession of ignorance the fathers return to their figure: Augustine says he is like one anointed but not yet able to see, who preaches and knows not what he preaches, and Bede makes him the catechumen, believing in Jesus but not strictly knowing him, not being yet washed. Henry ends with the plain fact that by the time he gained his sight he had lost his Physician, so that in the work of grace we see the change but not the hand that makes it, the way of the Spirit being like the wind, whose sound we hear without telling whence it comes.
13:
Who brought him, and why, is left open. Henry offers both readings — that some meant well, to show the Pharisees that the man they persecuted gave real proofs of a divine mission, or, likelier, that they meant to exasperate men already bitter enough, since persecuting rulers never want instruments to blow the coals. Lightfoot explains the name: in this Gospel the Pharisees generally stand for the Sanhedrin, and John never mentions Sadducees at all.

That the day was a sabbath is the whole case for the prosecution. Ellicott identifies it with the last great day of the feast and specifies two offences, kneading clay being servile work and anointing the eyes with spittle expressly forbidden, no healing being allowed except in immediate danger; Robertson observes this mattered to them far more than whether or how the thing was done. Henry asks why Christ healed on that day, and in a manner certain to offend, and gives three answers: he would not yield to a usurped authority whose zeal for rituals had consumed the substance of religion, he meant to expound the fourth commandment and clear it of their glosses, and he chose the day to dignify it.

The second questioning gets a shorter answer. Ellicott hears a man replying against his will who says no more than he must, and notes that do see is not what he said before, the phrase now claiming conscious possession; Barnes turns their procedure into a lasting reproach: the proper question was whether the thing had been done, not how, and it is remarkable how much of men's disputing concerns the mode by which the Spirit renews a heart rather than the evidence that it has. Calvin says they leave the fact aside and argue only the law, assuming an error refuted a hundred times, imputable only to obstinate malice.

The council divides, and both halves are examined. Augustine notes it was some and not all, for some were already anointed, and turns their charge round: to keep the sabbath spiritually is to have no sin, so they kept it carnally and transgressed it spiritually. Chrysostom observes that they pass over the miracle to give prominence to the supposed transgression, and that none dared say openly what he thought, one because the fact seemed improbable, another from love of position. Ellicott identifies the better party with Nicodemus, Joseph and perhaps Gamaliel; Robertson recognises the argument Nicodemus had used long before. Barnes builds on the silence of the other side: Celsus, Porphyry and Julian never denied the miracles but tried to account for them otherwise; Clarke adds that magicians might do things apparently miraculous but nothing really good, and one might safely defy all Egypt's magicians to open a single blind man's eyes.

Calvin will not let the argument from miracles stand unqualified, and produces a pagan parallel. Suetonius relates that at Alexandria a blind man asked Vespasian to anoint his eyes with spittle, having been so directed by Serapis in a dream, and the eyes were instantly opened — yet who would reckon Vespasian among the servants of God? Calvin does not think the story fabulous but ascribes it to a righteous vengeance, the Jews who despised Christ's miracles being justly given over to Satan's counterfeits. When the man is asked again, John Chrysostom notices the question is now about the opened eyes rather than the broken sabbath, and infers the speakers are the seceding party, producing the man to silence their opponents without appearing partisan; Theophylact reads the same good intent, Augustine the opposite, that they sought a handle to cast him out. All admire the answer: Chrysostom says the poor man speaks more wisely than any of them, Barnes calls it a noble confession made before the rulers, and Augustine, that not being yet anointed in heart he could not name the Son of God, yet was not wrong.
18:
Having failed to frighten the man, they send for his parents, and the move is thought self-defeating. Chrysostom says it is the nature of truth to be strengthened by the snares laid against it, a lie being its own antagonist: the objection that the neighbours judged by a resemblance is cut off once parents are produced who can identify their own son. Ellicott adds that they hoped fear would draw from them a denial of either the identity or the blindness from birth. Robertson says bluntly they called the parents in to cover their own stupidity, and Calvin that their unbelief was voluntary — nothing hindered them from seeing an obvious work of God but the malice that keeps the eyes shut.

Three questions are put as one. Robertson calls the compound shrewd, framed to confuse and furnish a handle; Ellicott hears the emphatic pronoun — ye say he was born blind, as against us, who do not believe it — and finds in the word rendered now the suddenness of the change. Theophylact sets out their intended dilemma: either he does not now see, or he was not blind before, and since the seeing is plain the blindness must be denied. Chrysostom asks with indignation what father would say such a thing of his son if it were untrue, and why they did not put their real charge, whom you made blind.

The parents answer two and decline the third. Chrysostom notes that the refusal itself completes the proof, the inquiry now resting on the healed man's own confession, and Robertson that the two admissions cut the ground from under the denial, so the Pharisees failed here. Augustine glosses the referral wittily — we might justly be compelled to speak for an infant who cannot speak, but this man, blind from birth, was never dumb. Henry turns their frank avowal into a reproof of those ashamed of a child's infirmity, since these owned him though he was born blind and lived on alms.

Their caution is not admired. Chrysostom asks what gratitude conceals what it knows from fear; Alcuin notes the Evangelist shows the answer came not from ignorance but fear, and Theophylact contrasts the fainthearted parents with their son, that intrepid witness whose understanding God had enlightened. Henry is severest, that they were bound in gratitude to speak for the Lord who had shown their son such kindness and had not courage, and that in a day of trial the man not apparently for Christ is justly reckoned against him — near is my friend, and near my child, and perhaps near my religion, but nearer is myself. He finds a better use in the phrase they hid behind: while children cannot speak, parents must speak for them, to God in prayer and to the church in baptism, but once they are of age it is fit they be asked whether they will stand to it.

What they feared is set out precisely. Barnes describes two grades of excommunication — the lighter shutting a man out for thirty days and keeping him four cubits from wife and friends, the heavier a perpetual exclusion with maledictions, called the curse, so complete that none might sell him the necessaries of life — and judges it was dread of the second that silenced them. Augustine dismisses the threat in a sentence: it was no disadvantage to be put out of the synagogue, since whom they cast out Christ took in. Henry draws the rule, that the fear of man brings a snare and makes people disown Christ against their consciences, and closes with the contrast the chapter is built on — the unlearned and poor, being simple-hearted, draw the proper inference from the light of the gospel, while those whose desires lie another way are ever learning and never come to the knowledge of the truth.
24:
The formula they open with is not what it sounds like, and on this the commentators are unanimous. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin all identify give glory to God as a form of adjuration, the words Joshua used to Achan when putting him on oath; Ellicott adds that the phrase is generally misread as a call to trace the cure to its source, which is impossible here, since the speakers assume no cure took place. Robertson notes they wish to settle a question of fact by authority, as persecutors have in every age. Calvin exposes the double move — a plausible preface exhorting him to honour God, followed at once by a prohibition against answering according to his conviction, so that under pretence of God's name they demand servile obedience — and turns aside to the oath itself, that men who forget they deny God when they invoke him to uphold a falsehood have filled every place with perjuries. Augustine puts it shortest: to deny the benefit received is not to give God glory but to blaspheme him.

The reply is guarded, and its guardedness is variously explained. Alcuin says he answered so as neither to expose himself to calumny nor conceal the truth. Chrysostom asks how the man who called him a prophet can now profess not to know whether he is a sinner, and answers that this was judgment, not fear: the defence lay better in the fact than in his own pleading. Calvin and Barnes both hear irony, a man who confessed him a prophet and gained nothing by it now suspending judgment on the person to press the fact harder. Ellicott dwells on the phrase one thing, which marks the chief matter so plainly that every other is excluded; Robertson finds him keen and quick, refusing the trap.

Asking again how it was done is treated as a confession of defeat. Alcuin says that being unable to overturn the fact they fall back on their former ground, following the scent like hounds, and notes they ask not how he came to see but how his eyes were opened, hoping he might detract from the operation; Barnes thinks the repetition meant to draw him into contradiction. Alcuin marks the change of tone — gentle while the matter wanted examining, bolder once the victory was won. Augustine reads the retort as it stands: I am his disciple already, do you wish to be? He sees now, and does not envy, no longer able to tolerate blindness in others. Chrysostom generalises: truth is strength and falsehood weakness, so truth ennobles whomever it takes up, however mean before, while falsehood brings even the strong to contempt.

Their answer is abuse, and Augustine will not let it stand as abuse. Thou art his disciple is a curse only in the intention of the speakers, not in the words themselves — may such a curse be upon us and upon our children. Against their appeal to Moses he sets Christ's own word, that had they believed Moses they would have believed him, since Moses wrote of him: do you follow the servant and turn your back on the Lord?

Henry turns the man's one certainty into the pattern of a testimony. Christ's mercies are most valued by those who have felt the want of them, and the strongest affection for him rises from knowledge rather than argument; so in the work of grace, though we cannot tell when or by what steps the change was wrought, we may take its comfort if we can say that whereas I was blind, now I see. Robertson enters the caution that at this stage the man did not yet know who Jesus was; and Henry adds the darker half, that the unbelief of men who enjoy every means of conviction is the thing truly to be marvelled at.
30:
The man now takes the offensive. Ellicott prefers the reading the marvellous thing and hears the sting in the pronoun — ye whose business it is to know, who claim special knowledge of just such questions. Robertson finds him angry at last and quick in reply: you confess ignorance, you who know everything, and yet he opened my eyes; the stubborn fact stands. Wesley marvels that a man utterly illiterate should argue with such strength and clearness, as though God had opened the eyes of his understanding along with the others.

What follows is a formal argument, and Ellicott sets it out in three steps: God hears not sinners but only those who worship him and do his will; that God hears this man is certain, since such a miracle needs divine power; therefore this man is not a sinner but from God. Robertson calls the conclusion inevitable, and says the man has scored with terrific power in his use of Scripture and logic.

The premise itself is the difficulty, and here they part company. Barnes hedges it with qualifications: the words have no reference to the prayers sinners make for salvation, and would not be true if they had, being the opinion of a man who was not inspired; the only prayers God refuses are those offered in mockery or by one unwilling to give up his sins. Ellicott warns that men have lifted the sentence out of its context and read into it a darkness it cannot bear, since no words of God set a limit to a grace that reaches every penitent. Calvin refuses that softening: those who think the man merely echoed popular opinion are mistaken, for it is the uniform doctrine of Scripture that God listens to none but such as call upon him in truth, the prayer of the wicked being an abomination, so the ungodly profane his name by praying and deserve punishment rather than an answer. Clarke offers a way between, taking the word to mean heathen, those not proselyted, set over against a worshipper of the true God; Wesley limits it to the impenitent, adding that the man's courage in adhering to the truth, knowing the penalty, earns him the title of confessor.

On the claim that nothing like it was ever heard, two of them reach for modern surgery. Barnes and Clarke both report that sight was never restored to one born blind by natural means until 1728, when Cheselden couched the eyes of a young man of fourteen, and both infer that the difficulty of the operation with the best skill available measures the greatness of what was done here without any operation. Ellicott meets the objection in advance: that modern science can now do it is beside the question, unless it is pretended human skill could do it under the same conditions and by the same means.

Their answer is to reproach him with the very thing he was healed of. Chrysostom observes that so long as they expected a denial they were willing to believe him, and cast him out only when he would not give it, and that in pronouncing his blindness the fruit of his sins they reason most unreasonably. Augustine notes the ingratitude precisely: they had made him their teacher by questioning him so often, and now expel him for teaching; and on the word altogether, that it means he was wholly blind, yet he who opened his eyes saves him altogether too. John Chrysostom turns the expulsion into a promise: those who suffer for the confession of Christ are the most honoured of men, for the Jews cast this one out of the Temple and the Lord of the Temple found him, parted from a pestilent company and meeting the Fountain of salvation, dishonoured by those who dishonoured Christ and honoured by the Lord of angels.
35:
The finding is treated as deliberate, not accidental. Chrysostom says the Evangelist means us to see that Christ came on purpose to say this, receiving him as a judge receives the wrestler after his labours and crowns him; and he puts the sense of the question in Christ's mouth — the people have heaped reproaches on me and I care nothing for them, one thing only I care for, that you should believe. Henry works it into a rule: earthly princes cannot notice everyone who defends them, but Christ observes every faithful testimony borne to him, and persecutors who shut a good man out of their communion cannot shut him out of communion with Christ — happy are they who have a friend from whom men cannot debar them.

Hilary presses the exact form of the question. Had any confession of Christ been the perfection of faith, the words would have been, dost thou believe in Christ; but since heretics have that name readily in their mouths, confessing Christ while denying the Son, what belongs to Christ alone is asked of faith — and it profits nothing to believe on the Son of God as a creature rather than a Son. Chrysostom reads the counter-question as the speech of a longing mind: he does not yet know the one for whom he contended so hard, itself a proof of his love of truth, since he was blind before he came to his benefactor and seized by the Jews immediately after. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the word rendered Lord means no more here than Sir, the ordinary address to a prophet, and Calvin cautions that what is reached at this point is a very small and cold portion of faith, a beginning from which Christ meant to lead him further.

The answer takes a road neither direct nor obscure. Chrysostom notes that Christ does not say, I am he who healed thee, but takes a middle way of speaking; Theophylact hears in thou hast seen him a reminder of the cure that gave him power to see, and adds a caution against Nestorius, that he who speaks was born of Mary and the son is the Son of God, not two persons. Henry observes that Christ revealed himself so plainly to almost no one else — this man and the woman of Samaria — leaving others to reach it by argument, and that the man was asking where the Saviour was at the very moment he spoke with him, as doubting believers still ask where the Lord is when it is he who talks with them.

What the man had gained by his eyesight is turned over. Henry finds the chief comfort of bodily sight in its usefulness to faith, so this man might have gone back to blindness contentedly, like old Simeon, having seen the salvation of God. He notes too that the man disputes nothing said by one who had shown such mercy, so that the bruised reed has become a cedar.

The confession ends in an act rather than a word. Augustine marks the sequence: first the face of the heart is washed, and then, the conscience being cleansed, he acknowledges as Son of God the one he had already owned as Son of man. I believe, he says, is a small thing — would you see what he believes of him? and falling down, he worshipped him. Chrysostom makes the deed added to the word a plain acknowledgment of divine power, and Henry the same: since none but God may be worshipped, in worshipping Jesus he owned him God. Bede takes the posture for a lesson in prayer: not to pray with uplifted neck but prostrate on the earth, suppliantly imploring mercy. Henry closes by noting we never read of the man again, though it is likely he became from that hour a constant follower.
39:
The word judgment has to be rescued from the obvious sense. Barnes points out that condemnation cannot be meant, since Christ elsewhere denies he came to condemn the world, and reads it as declaring men's condition, with the effect that some are reformed and some more deeply condemned — an effect, not a design. Ellicott notes that the Greek word John uses only here means not the act of judging but the sentence that follows it, so Christ's coming brought light into the darkness of men's hearts by which false and true were tested: the light judged no man, and yet by it every man was judged. Augustine said the same, that this act of division is what is called judgment, not that by which he will judge the quick and the dead at the end of the world.

How both halves of the saying can be true is worked out by the same figure. Ellicott insists the two phrases are read from the speakers' point of view — that they which think they see not might really see, and they which think they see might really be made blind. Henry applies it first to nations, the Gentiles seeing a great light while blindness happens to Israel, then to persons, since Christ came designedly to give sight to the spiritually blind and, in the event, left sealed in ignorance those who set their own wisdom against revelation. Chrysostom reaches for Paul's formulation, that the Gentiles who followed not after righteousness attained it, while Israel, following after the law of righteousness, did not.

Chrysostom insists on the distinction the Pharisees miss. There is a twofold sight and a twofold blindness, of the senses and of the understanding, and these men were intent only on things of sense and ashamed only of blindness of the eyes; so Christ shows them it were better to be blind than to see as they saw. Theophylact sets the two side by side — the man who saw nothing from birth now sees in body and soul, while those who seem to see have had their understanding darkened. Gill finds the same doubling in the word, a judgment inflicting judicial blindness on some while in mercy illuminating others.

Their question is heard as an outburst of wounded rank. Henry catches what stung: they took Christ to mean the seers of the people, who valued themselves on insight and foresight, and so protest — the common people are blind, but are we blind also, the rabbis, the doctors, the learned in the law? He calls it a libel on the great, and remarks that those who most need reproof often have wit enough to detect a tacit one and not grace enough to bear a just one, nothing fortifying a corrupt heart against the word so effectually as the high opinion others hold of it.

The answer is read as a diagnosis rather than a sentence. Augustine gives it plainly: if you called yourselves blind and ran to the physician you would have no sin, but saying we see, you do not seek a physician, and so remain in your blindness. Henry doubles the thought — had they been really ignorant the guilt would have been less, invincible ignorance excusing though not justifying, and had they known themselves blind they would have taken Christ for guide — so the very thing they gloried in is their ruin, there being no greater hindrance to a soul's salvation than self-sufficiency. He presses the medical figure: no patients are so hard to manage as those in a frenzy who say nothing ails them, and the sin of the self-confident remains because they reject the gospel of grace, its guilt unpardoned and its power unbroken. Theophylact allows a gentler reading, that ignorance of the Scriptures would have made the offence lighter, but calling themselves wise in the law, they condemn themselves.
